We report a 32-year-old patient with stiff-man syndrome and anti-GAD antibodies who developed subacute progressive loss of vision in the right eye, and in the left eye 18 months thereafter.
The patient’s symptoms began at the age of 14 years with progressive stiffness and hyperlordosis of the lower spine.

Standard serological studies, glucose tolerance tests and repeat spinal taps yielded normal results except for one oligoclonal band in the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) on the second tap in 1996.
Cranial computerized tomography (CT), magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the cranium and spine, and thoracic myelography were all normal.
The patient died in 1997, about 12 h after a spasm-induced fall involving head trauma.

Relief of spasms was achieved with clonazepam. Despite cessation of medication, the patient remained free of spasms over the following 3 years. Spasms and involuntary jerks reappeared at the age of 23, but could be controlled with diazepam (5–10 mg per week). Gradual drug tolerance, however, necessitated increasingly higher dosages (80–100 mg/day).
Despite aggressive immunosuppressive treatment with i.v. steroids and methotrexate, progression of visual loss in the left eye could not be prevented.
